newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen loser backs Maskhadov presidential win.
newsitem.headline: Chechen loser backs Maskhadov presidential win.

text.p: Chechen rebel Shamil Basayev, Russia's most wanted "terrorist", conceded defeat on Wednesday in the separatist region's presidential election and endorsed the victory of senior guerrilla commander Aslan Maskhadov.

Preliminary results from Monday's election gave Maskhadov, who commanded the tiny guerrilla army that forced Russian troops out of Chechnya last year, 64.8 percent of the vote to Basayev's 22.7 percent.

Central Electoral Commission chairman Mumadi Saydaiyev told a news conference that acting separatist president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev was third on 10.2 percent, with votes from seven small, remote districts out of a total of 63 yet to be counted.
Maskhadov had claimed victory on Tuesday and immediately promised to reopen talks with Russia on recognition of Chechen sovereignty and on demands for war reparations from Moscow.

In Moscow, President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told Itar-Tass news agency the Kremlin had no grounds to question the legitimacy of Monday's election but reiterated Russian opposition to Chechen independence.

Maskhadov, a 45-year-old former Soviet artillery colonel, promised to restore order to the mainly Moslem region and reunite the secessionist guerrilla movement after its leaders campaigned against each other in the election.
Basayev, 32, whom Maskhadov forgave on Tuesday for running a dirty campaign, ruled out any "split" and said he would not oppose the man who had been his leader during the war.
He announced he would quit politics for the computer business.
"I won't get in his way," Basayev said at his headquarters in the devastated Minutka area of the Chechen capital Grozny.
"I will get on with my own private life. I will get on with business, the computer business," he added.
Basayev is wanted in Russia for "terrorism" after a bloody hostage-taking raid on the Russian town of Budennovsk in 1995 in which more than 100 people were killed.
Surveying the post-election scene, Maskhadov has much to be proud of as he prepares to form a new government.

The Chechens have won international sympathy for their sufferings in a war started by Yeltsin, which killed tens of thousands. They humiliated the Russian army and have chosen a separatist leader in a vote judged "legitimate" by foreign monitors.

International observers strongly praised the election on Wednesday. "What we saw was democracy against a backdrop of ruins," said Poland's Tadeusz Iwinski, vice-president of the Council of Europe's observer team.

Ivan Rybkin, secretary of Russia's policy-making Security Council, hailed the poll as a further step towards peace and stability in the turbulent Caucasian region and told reporters Russia was ready to resume negotiations.

But for all the stunning success of Maskhadov's military and electoral campaigns, the political and economic task facing the soft-spoken rebel leader is a daunting one and Russia still holds many strong cards.
Maskhadov himself admitted on Tuesday: "Our economic situation is woeful...nearly everything has been destroyed."
The silver-haired commander demanded reparations from Russia and said he plans to negotiate a share of revenues from lucrative Russian oil pipelines that cross Chechen territory.
Moscow has promised reconstruction aid and has offered a share of oil profits to tempt the Chechens out of seceding.
Surrounded on three sides by Russian territory and with its back to the soaring Caucasus mountains, landlocked Chechnya under Maskhadov has turned abroad for recognition.

But the tiny nation of one million may find it hard to win real support since Western countries have no interest in seeing Russia start to break up. And Moscow has threatened to sever ties with any country that acknowledges Chechen sovereignty.
